title: Product categories
audience: Trainee or new worker on the window cleaning (all heights) track, working under supervision.
learningOutcomes: Distinguish detergents, degreasers, descalers, disinfectants and specialist products by function and approved use.
Identify the soil and substrate before choosing a product category.
Explain why a disinfectant does not replace removal of heavy visible soil.

instruction.heading: Exterior, height and access context
instruction.body: This lesson is part of the window cleaning (all heights) track. The track covers ground-level, water-fed pole and elevated access work on glazing and frames. Any work above ground level, or from a ladder, scaffold or elevating work platform, is restricted: it needs employer authorisation under a site-specific risk assessment, and the worker must hold any licence the relevant state or territory requires for the equipment used. This lesson does not grant the right to work at height or on solar systems.

instruction.heading: Learning goal and job context
instruction.body: This lesson teaches product categories for routine cleaning work. Start with the actual job scope, site instructions, manufacturer directions and worker training. Never treat a general lesson as authority to perform restricted or specialist work.

instruction.heading: Core procedure
instruction.body: Distinguish detergents, degreasers, descalers, disinfectants and specialty products by intended task, not marketing language. Identify the soil and substrate before choosing a category. A disinfectant is not a substitute for removing heavy visible soil unless an approved combined process specifically allows it.

instruction.heading: Decision-making in the field
instruction.body: Before acting, ask: What is the surface or equipment? What is the soil or hazard? Which product or method is approved? What could harm a person, property or food? If the answer is unclear, pause, protect the area and seek supervisor guidance.

instruction.heading: Worked workplace scenario
instruction.body: A worker chooses a descaler for grease on a painted cupboard. The trainer explains why a compatible degreaser and material check are needed.

instruction.heading: Guided supervised practice
instruction.body: Sort twelve product labels into categories and match each to an authorised cleaning scenario and exclusion.

instruction.heading: Evidence and feedback
instruction.body: The assessor observes the task and checks whether the learner: explains product purpose and avoids substituting incompatible categories. A learner must explain any unsafe choice, correct it and repeat the demonstration. Record observations, required coaching and reassessment rather than awarding competence from attendance alone.

instruction.heading: Stop-work rule
instruction.body: Stop-work rule: stop immediately, make the area safe, and tell your supervisor before resuming if the surface, anchor, ladder, platform or roof is unstable or uncertain; wind, rain, ice or fading light changes conditions; you see or suspect exposed wiring, damaged cable, water near electrical equipment or live parts; a person or animal enters the exclusion zone; the task falls outside your training, authorisation or the work order; or you are asked to work above ground level without the licence or authorisation required.

procedure: Identify the surface or equipment, and the soil or hazard, before choosing a product.
Check the product label and the manufacturer's directions against the approved method for the job.
Match each product category to its intended task, not to marketing language.
Check that the product is compatible with the surface before use.
Do not use a disinfectant in place of removing heavy visible soil, unless an approved combined process allows it.
Do not substitute incompatible categories for one another.
If the choice is unclear, pause, protect the area and seek supervisor guidance.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: Licence and height notice: This lesson does not grant the right to work at height, on roofs, from elevated work platforms, or on solar systems. Completing it is not a licence, certificate or authority for regulated work. Boom-type elevating work platforms need a high risk work licence in Victoria at any boom length, and in New South Wales, Queensland, Tasmania, the Northern Territory and Western Australia where the boom is 11 metres or more. The WorkSafe WA page (last updated 13 August 2026) and the NT WorkSafe bulletin (no date shown) both state the 11-metre threshold. Check whether this work needs a high-risk work licence with the state regulator before you start. Queensland's definition does not cover platforms under 11 metres (WorkSafe Queensland page, no date shown). Tasmania's WP licence applies where the boom length is 11 metres or more, and no licence is needed for a boom under 11 metres (WorkSafe Tasmania page, last updated 1 December 2023). In New South Wales and Queensland the boom length is 11 metres: a boom-type platform of 11 metres or more needs the licence, and a shorter boom may not need it in those states. Victoria's WP class has no boom-length threshold, so the licence is not limited by length there. This lesson does not grant a licence. Scissor lifts need no high risk work licence in Victoria or the Northern Territory. Check the licence rules for your state or territory and obtain your employer's written authorisation before any work above ground level.

Stop-work rule: stop immediately, make the area safe, and tell your supervisor before resuming if the surface, anchor, ladder, platform or roof is unstable or uncertain; wind, rain, ice or fading light changes conditions; you see or suspect exposed wiring, damaged cable, water near electrical equipment or live parts; a person or animal enters the exclusion zone; the task falls outside your training, authorisation or the work order; or you are asked to work above ground level without the licence or authorisation required.

knowledgeChecks.question: What should you check before performing product categories?
options: The marketing claim on the front of the bottle, the box, the label, the price and the logo
The soil and substrate, and the product's intended task rather than its marketing language
The product's fragrance, to match the room, the décor and the client's taste
Whether it is the strongest product on the shelf in the store, the van and the depot

knowledgeChecks.question: What do you do when the right product category for grease is uncertain?
options: Choose the strongest category to be sure
Mix two categories to cover both risks
Use a descaler on the grease, since it looks similar to a degreaser
Pause, protect the area and seek supervisor guidance

knowledgeChecks.question: Which product category suits greasy soil on a painted cupboard?
options: Use a descaler, since it is the strongest product on the trolley
Use the disinfectant at full strength on the cupboard
Use the nearest bottle, since the label category matters little
Use a compatible degreaser after a material check, rather than a descaler

knowledgeChecks.question: Which product choice is unsafe when heavy visible soil is present?
options: Using a degreaser after a material check on the surface
Checking the surface before choosing a product for the job
Stopping to ask when unsure about the product choice
Using a disinfectant in place of removing heavy visible soil

knowledgeChecks.question: What should be recorded when a cleaning product is chosen?
options: No record is needed for product choice on the job, the cart or the bin
A note of the brand name only, on the label, the box, the cart and the shelf
Record the product choice, the surface, and any coaching or reassessment needed
A verbal account to the next shift at the start of the day and the job
